c.tagline: Iraq's holy city of the golden shrine, cradle of Shia pilgrimage.

taxi.fareNote: No ride-hailing apps operate; getting around is by street and shared taxis with the fare agreed before the ride. Carry small IQD notes and confirm the price up front.

emergency.note: 104 reaches the police and 122 the ambulance service; Najaf is a holy city where alcohol is banned and modest dress is expected, especially around the shrine.

avoid.reason: Avoid the desert outskirts and intercity roads after dark due to checkpoints and residual security risks; stay within the city and shrine area.
Expect dense crowds and pickpocketing risk around the Imam Ali Shrine during pilgrimage periods, and dress conservatively at all times.

hood_desc: The historic core wrapped around the gold-domed Imam Ali Shrine, one of Shia Islam's holiest sites; a dense warren of hotels, bookshops, and eateries where pilgrims can reach the shrine on foot at any hour. Best for first-time visitors who want to be steps from the sanctuary.
The commercial heart of Najaf a short walk or ride from the shrine, buzzing with markets, restaurants, and shops; a practical base that balances shrine access with everyday city life and services.

A more upscale, spread-out district with newer hotels and business facilities away from the shrine crowds; suits travelers who want quieter, more modern accommodation and don't mind a short taxi ride to the old city.

The adjoining town of Kufa on the Euphrates, about 10 km northeast, home to the historic Great Mosque of Kufa and a calmer riverside setting; good for visitors drawn to the area's early Islamic history.

A quieter residential belt along the road toward Karbala and beside the vast Wadi us-Salaam cemetery, with budget-friendly hotels and a slower pace; suits families and longer-staying pilgrims wanting lower prices.

water.note: Drink only bottled or filtered water.

transit.hours: Shared taxis and minibuses run roughly from early morning until late evening; there is no fixed schedule and taxis fill the late-night gap.
transit.note: Najaf has no metro, tram, or rail transit; getting around relies on shared taxis, private taxis, and minibuses, with the shrine area best explored on foot.
transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash (Iraqi dinar) directly to the driver; there is no rechargeable transit card. Agree the fare before setting off and carry small notes.

tip.r: Not customary; rounding up the bill or leaving small change for good service is appreciated but not expected.

landmarks: Imam Ali Shrine (Haram of Imam Ali)
The dazzling gold-domed mausoleum of Imam Ali, first Shia Imam, draws millions of pilgrims and glows with mirrored halls and intricate tilework.
Wadi al-Salam Cemetery (Valley of Peace)
One of the world's largest cemeteries, this vast sea of tombs and turquoise domes stretches for miles and holds centuries of Shia burials.
Great Mosque of Kufa
Among Islam's oldest mosques, this seventh-century sanctuary in nearby Kufa marks where Imam Ali was struck down and shelters revered shrines within its walls.
Old City Souq (Grand Bazaar of Najaf)
A labyrinth of covered lanes beside the shrine, fragrant with spices and prayer beads, where pilgrims and traders have haggled for centuries.
Al-Sahla Mosque
A sprawling fortress-like mosque on Kufa's edge, venerated in Shia tradition as a future refuge of the Mahdi and beautifully lit after dusk.
Shrine of Muslim ibn Aqil
Adjoining the Kufa Mosque, this golden-domed tomb honors Imam Hussein's envoy, whose martyrdom presaged Karbala and stirs deep devotion among visitors.
House of Imam Ali (Dar al-Imam Ali, Kufa)
A humble restored courtyard house near the Kufa Mosque where Imam Ali is said to have lived, offering an intimate counterpoint to the grand shrines.
Al-Hannana Mosque
A cherished blue-tiled mosque on the Kufa road where, tradition says, the pillars wept as Imam Ali's funeral procession passed by.
Bahr al-Najaf (Sea of Najaf)
A shallow seasonal lake and depression west of the city, its palm-fringed shores and desert sunsets give Najaf its most photogenic natural escape.
Amir al-Mu'minin Library (Haydariyya Library)
A storied seminary library near the shrine, safeguarding rare Islamic manuscripts and embodying Najaf's thousand-year role as a center of Shia scholarship.

dom.op: Iraqi Republic Railways (IRR) — tickets sold at station ticket offices only; there is no online booking

train.note: Najaf lies on the reopened line that runs south-west from Baghdad through Karbala, and Iraqi Republic Railways operates occasional services, with extra pilgrim trains at Ashura and Arbaeen; frequencies are low and schedules are not published online, so tickets are bought at the station. In practice almost all visitors reach Najaf by air into Al Najaf International Airport, which handles flights from Baghdad and several Iranian cities as well as Istanbul and Dubai, or by road from Baghdad and Karbala. There are no international passenger trains anywhere in Iraq.

intl.to: Mehran & Tehran, Qom, Mashhad (Iran) - pilgrimage coaches via the Mehran/Zurbatiyah and Shalamcheh/Basra crossings
intl.op: Iranian and Iraqi pilgrimage coach operators — booked through pilgrimage agencies rather than online

bus.note: Buses and shared taxis leave from garages on the edge of town and run constantly to Karbala (about 80 km, 1.5 hours), Baghdad (about 3 hours) and Basra, with fares paid to the driver and no online booking. Najaf and Karbala are effectively a single pilgrimage circuit, and shared cars shuttle between them all day and night. Iranian pilgrims arrive in very large numbers by coach through the Mehran border, and around Arbaeen the roads between Najaf, Karbala and the Iranian frontier are given over to the walking pilgrimage, with long delays and diversions for everyone else.

ferry.note: Najaf is an inland desert city with no seaport and no navigable river, so no ferry or boat services operate.
